db_evidence.notes: The fight's location/time window is trivially findable (entities:000208 'kang jinlong (亢金龙), white dragon boss' spans 23430-23730, matched by semantic_search and by event_steps). But no memory table (episodes, visual_clips, semantic_triples, event_steps, object_states) ever contains the phrase 'perfect dodge' or an equivalent structured record for this interval — the 30-second visual_clips captions only say the character 'dodges', 'dashes', or 'evades' generically, never distinguishing the perfect-dodge mechanic (a brief visual flash/afterimage effect) from ordinary dodges. So the count is not retrievable from the DB at all; it can only come from frame-level visual inspection via clip_qa, and every rollout's clip_qa undercounted (1, 2, or 3 events per pass) against the reference 6.

root_causes: The perfect-dodge visual effect appears to be brief (evidenced by rollout-01 needing a 10fps zoom on a ~1.2s window to confirm a single event), so any coarse fps sampling (1fps or even 4fps) across a 270s fight window can miss most occurrences between sampled frames.

clip_qa calls are budget-limited (rollout-01 shows images_used climbing from 270 to 1013 with remaining_images dropping to single digits), forcing the sub-agent to leave large portions of the interval at coarse fps or skip zoom-in entirely once budget is exhausted.

Rollouts that split the interval into 2-3 sub-windows per clip_qa call (rollout-00, rollout-02) still only found 1 event per sub-window on average, suggesting the visual detector itself (not just sampling density) is unreliable at recognizing the perfect-dodge effect versus an ordinary dodge/roll.

No rollout used a systematic, densely-sampled full-interval pass (e.g. exhaustive 2-4fps across the whole 245s span) combined with a stitched double-check across sub-window boundaries; several stopped after a single clip_qa call and directly summed or accepted partial-window counts.
DB text at the granularities available (30sec visual_clips) never encodes 'perfect dodge' as a distinguishable label, so there was no textual shortcut to cross-validate the visual count.
what_worked: All 5 rollouts correctly located the Kang-Jin Loong fight interval (23430-23730) via semantic_search/entities/event_steps, so temporal localization itself was not the failure.
All rollouts correctly recognized that this count requires clip_qa (visual verification) rather than trusting DB text, and did invoke it.

Some rollouts (00, 02) attempted to split the long interval into sub-windows to increase effective sampling density, which is the right general strategy even though it wasn't executed densely enough here.
transferable_lessons: For counting-type questions over a brief, repeatable visual effect across a long interval (~250s here), a single clip_qa call at low fps is insufficient; the interval should be tiled into short (~20-30s) sub-windows each sampled at a fps high enough to catch a sub-second effect, and the sub-window counts should be summed with de-duplication at boundaries.

When clip_qa's image budget is a hard constraint, prioritize dense sampling over the full target interval rather than spending budget on speculative coarse-then-zoom passes that leave most of the interval under-sampled.

When two independent clip_qa calls over overlapping/adjacent windows return conflicting or partial counts, don't just take the first or sum blindly — reconcile by re-inspecting boundary regions and by checking whether the effect's visual signature (color/duration) is consistent across all claimed events.

If the DB never contains the exact terminology of the question's target event, don't just proceed straight to one clip_qa call; treat this as a strong signal that the visual sub-agent must be used exhaustively (dense multi-window tiling) rather than as a quick confirmation step.
open_questions: The reference answer '6 times' was not independently re-derived by exhaustively re-watching the full fight frame-by-frame in this diagnosis; it is trusted as given, but given how inconsistent and low all 5 rollout counts are (1-4), it's worth someone visually re-verifying the reference count against the source video to rule out the reference itself being an overcount from a different counting convention (e.g. counting near-misses or partial dodges as 'perfect').

Whether the game's perfect-dodge effect has a consistent, learnable visual signature (color/duration) that the visual sub-agent model is simply bad at recognizing, versus the failure being purely a sampling-density problem, was not disambiguated here.
